source_text: Tu autem hebetior, qui fructum concupiscentiae diabolicae hominem dicens, Dei tamen eum ascribis operibus, non quasi de malo bonum factum, sed malum et de mala radice prolatum, habere tamen auctorem bonum, quem fructum radicis suae diabolus sibi vindicet.
pass_a_gloss: But you more dull, who saying a human the fruit of diabolical desire, nevertheless ascribe him to the works of God, not as if a good made from evil, but evil and brought forth from an evil root, yet to have a good author, which fruit of his own root the devil vindicates to himself.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae

pass_b_english: You are duller: you call a human being the fruit of diabolical desire, yet assign him to God’s works. You do not say he was made good from evil, but that he is evil and produced from an evil root, yet has a good author—while the devil claims him as the fruit of his own root (Matthew 7:17–18).

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Augustine's quoted claim that the unbaptized remain under the devil; keep the personal devil, not 'evil'.
rejected: under Satan (name not in the Latin here)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: An evil root and its evil fruit may echo the tree-and-fruit comparison.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
